sailing-alone-around-the-world: Between 1895 and 1898, retired sea captain Joshua Slocum did what no one had ever done: he sailed around the world alone. His little sloop Spray carried him 46,000 miles through storms, pirates, and long lonely weeks at sea. Written with dry humor and a sailor's eye for weather and waves, this true story remains the classic account of single-handed voyaging.
the-junior-classics-volume-5-stories-tha: William Patten's Junior Classics were designed to put the world's best stories into children's hands, and this fifth volume collects tales meant to be loved for a lifetime. Fairy tales, fables, and adventure stories appear in versions trimmed for young readers. Generations of families read these volumes aloud together, making the series one of the most cherished children's libraries of the early 1900s.
round-the-world: Before he became the world's richest man, steel magnate Andrew Carnegie took a grand tour of the globe — and wrote this lively memoir of the journey. From London to India to Japan, he reports on the people, railways, and wonders he met with a businessman's curiosity. The book shows a young industrialist discovering the wider world he would soon help reshape.
flowing-gold: Rex Beach strikes black gold in this novel of the oil boom, where fortunes rise and fall with each new well. Wildcatters, promoters, and the men who work the rigs clash in a story of greed, grit, and sudden wealth. Beach knew the world of boomtowns firsthand, and his tale of the petroleum frontier became a hit on the page and later on screen.
facing-the-world: Horatio Alger's formula made him the bestselling boys' author of the 1800s, and this story follows the familiar, beloved pattern. A poor but honest boy faces the world alone, and through hard work, courage, and integrity earns his rise. Generations of young Americans took Alger's heroes as models of what determination could achieve.
the-story-of-a-child: French novelist Pierre Loti recalls his own childhood in this lyrical memoir — a sensitive boy growing up in a quiet seaside town, dreaming of distant lands. His earliest impressions of nature, family, and the sea unfold in prose of great beauty. The book reveals the roots of the wanderlust that would fill his famous travel novels.
a-domestic-problem-work-and-culture-in-t: Reformer Abby Morton Diaz tackles the great Victorian question: how should a household be run? Work, servants, children, and culture all come under her sensible, progressive eye. Written with warmth and common sense, the book shows one thoughtful woman's plan for making home life both efficient and humane.
this-simian-world: Clarence Day — beloved humorist of Life with Father — looks at human society through the eyes of apes in this witty satire. Our customs, wars, and follies appear delightfully absurd from the simian point of view. Clever, humane, and quietly subversive.
prose-idylls-new-and-old: Charles Kingsley gathers prose idylls — short, lovely pieces on nature, country life, and the sea, old and new. His muscular Christian warmth colors every page. Gentle, manly writing from a beloved Victorian parson. Short, sunlit pieces on woods, waters, and country folk, old favorites and new, glow with his hearty faith.
the-home-and-the-world: Rabindranath Tagore's great novel sets a Bengali woman between her devoted husband and a charismatic nationalist leader. Home and world, tradition and change, pull at her heart. The Nobel laureate's most searching work of fiction, profound and moving. Torn between love and cause, his heroine embodies a nation's painful awakening.
